title: Disabled parking: the practical family guide.
summary: Handicapped parking permits, nonvisible disabilities, passenger use and safer arrivals: a family guide with official links for MA, RI, NH, Maine and Vermont.
search: Caregiver tools · Access starts at arrivalDisabled parking: the practical family guide.A small placard. A more manageable arrival. Where to begin, what to ask, and the official forms for five New England states.October 16, 2026 · A researched family guideOriginal editorial illustration. Display a placard while parked; remove it before driving. Some outings begin before we reach the door. There is the car, the traffic, the distance across the lot, and the person beside us who needs support for that part of the day. A disability parking placard—often called a handicapped parking pass—can be a useful access tool for someone who qualifies. A shorter route or room to use mobility equipment can make an arrival more manageable. The need is not always obvious to a stranger looking across a parking lot. This guide gathers the official starting points for five New England states. Start with the state where the person lives, and take the current form to the clinician who understands their needs. Who can qualify? A wheelchair is not the only reason someone may qualify. State criteria can include specific walking limitations, certain heart or lung conditions, blindness, or qualifying neurological conditions. The details differ by state. A diagnosis by itself does not guarantee a placard. Autism, epilepsy, a nonvisible disability or a history of elopement should not be presented as automatic eligibility. Ask the clinician to explain the person's actual limitations and support needs against the state's criteria. The motor-vehicle agency decides the application. For example, Massachusetts lists specific eligibility conditions, including being unable to walk 200 feet without resting or needing another person's assistance to walk. Its application asks the clinician for a qualifying clinical diagnosis and supporting information. The person does not have to be the driver. A qualifying passenger, including a child, can have a placard. Apply in the name of the person with the disability, following the state's parent or guardian instructions. A placard belongs to that person; it is not a general parking privilege for the household. New Hampshire's application, for example, explains that a placard can travel with its holder in different vehicles and that the holder must be getting out when the vehicle uses an accessible space. Check the rules wherever you park, including local meter rules. When elopement is part of the picture For a person who qualifies, reducing the journey through a busy parking area may help the family manage an arrival. But a closer space does not guarantee a safe route, and a placard does not prevent elopement or replace supervision. Before opening the door, agree which adult is supporting the person and where you are going. Look at the actual path: moving cars, crossings and the entrance matter as much as distance. Keep familiar communication supports available, and use the person's established safety plan. For dedicated wandering-prevention and response planning, see the National Autism Association's free Be REDy booklets and AWAARE resources. Those are useful companions to a conversation with the person's care team. Find your state's application These links lead to official agencies and forms. Use their current instructions for eligibility, certification, submission and renewal. MassachusettsComplete the RMV application with the required healthcare-provider certification. Placards have no application fee. The RMV asks for the original completed application by mail and recommends keeping a copy; allow at least 30 business days for processing.RMV application instructions and current form → Rhode IslandThe DMV's disability-placard application requires physician certification. Temporary, long-term and permanent placards have different validity periods. Use the DMV's disability page and current new/renewal form for the appropriate application route.Rhode Island placards and application links → New HampshireNew Hampshire calls this Walking Disability Privileges. Form RDMV 130 includes the application, medical-certification section and practical questions about passenger use and renewals. The instructions describe applying by mail or at a DMV location.Official RDMV 130 application and instructions (PDF) → MaineMaine uses form PS-18 for disability plates and placards. The BMV explains qualifying limitations, medical certification, temporary and permanent credentials, and proper display. Its page also links the application.Maine BMV guide and application → VermontFor a permanent placard, begin with VD-120 and review the medical-report requirement, VS-113. Vermont provides a separate temporary-placard form. For a minor, the permanent application instructs families to use the child's name.Vermont placard information and forms → Connecticut and other statesUse the federal government's directory to find your state's motor-vehicle agency and its disability-parking application. Requirements from a neighboring state are not a substitute for your own state's rules.Find your official state motor-vehicle agency → A small checklist before applying Open the current official form and read the eligibility criteria. Describe the person's actual walking limitations and required assistance to their clinician, including safety concerns where relevant. Check both applicant and clinician sections for required signatures and dates. Keep a copy and submit it within the state's stated deadline. After approval, note the expiry date and read the display and use rules. Once the placard arrives Use it only for the person to whom it was issued. Display it as directed while parked and remove it from the mirror before driving. Keep the striped access aisle clear—it is space people need to enter and leave vehicles, not an extra parking space. If accessible spaces are occupied, ask the venue about an appropriate drop-off or another practical entrance. Keep the plan flexible. The point is to make room for the day you came to have. Official application pages and published instructions checked October 16, 2026. This is general family-planning information, not an eligibility determination or individualized medical or legal advice. Agencies can change forms and requirements; the current official instructions control. Explore related topicsThe journal / Family & caregiver tools Advocacy & inclusion

title: Wandering is the activity.
summary: Inside the Book Barn in Niantic, Connecticut: room to wander, browse and take your time, with real outing observations and useful visit notes.
search: The Book Barn, Niantic · from our family camera roll.The Book Barn · a family field noteWandering is the activity.Books, gardens and curious corners. An afternoon without a prescribed route. Come alongA bookstore with room around it.The Book Barn feels like someone forgot to put walls around a bookstore. Books outside, books inside, gardens and odd corners. Our plan leaves space for wandering and one promising shelf.Looking for practical details? From our family notebook · NianticA bookstore without a script.The Book Barn is technically a used bookstore, but that description is as incomplete as calling the Maine coast “some water.” It is books, yes, but also paths, porches, garden corners, little buildings, signs, animals and the gentle feeling that the rules of an ordinary shop have loosened their tie.That is what we love about it. You do not enter and immediately feel the pressure of a proper cultural outing. There is no single route through the experience, no exhibit you are supposed to appreciate in the correct order. Someone can browse mysteries. Someone else can stay outside. You can look at three shelves or thirty. The wandering is the activity.From the existing family notebook. The photograph is our own; the decorative illustrations are interpretations, not current venue photographs.A subject that catches your eye is a good place to begin.From the rest of our notebook +On our visit, the place felt almost designed for a family that does better when the day contains choices but not demands. We could move. We could separate and come back together. We could notice whatever caught our attention instead of trying to maintain one shared pace. The atmosphere did much of the work for us: old books, greenery, bits of shade, curious corners, that slightly eccentric New England conviction that a perfectly reasonable business can sprawl across a property like a village.It is also the sort of place that gives a camera roll some texture: not a row of posed smiles, but hands on book spines, a path disappearing around a corner, a funny sign, someone absorbed in something that caught their eye. Those are the photographs we tend to keep. They look like the day felt—interesting, a little untidy, and entirely our own. Books and animals belong to the story. This cat is an illustration.The find is part of itOne promising shelf.And used bookstores have another advantage: they make very small victories feel satisfying. You do not need a major purchase. Finding one strange title, one old cookbook, one book about a topic somebody loves—that is enough. The object becomes a souvenir without announcing itself as one.Browse. Wander. Step outside. Leave when you are ready.What stays with us is the feeling of permission. Browse. Wander. Step outside. Look at something else. Come back. Leave when you are ready. It is a place with texture rather than a schedule, and that makes it one of those rare stops where the grown-ups can genuinely enjoy themselves without needing everybody to enjoy it in exactly the same way.Family story retained from our earlier notes, memory and camera roll.
